archetype.name: Pocket Passer (second-year)
archetype.definition: A tall, rhythm-based passer who wins from the pocket on short and intermediate throws. He creates little with his legs: six scrambles in 224 dropbacks.

report.headline: Red-zone sharp, leaky between the 20s: turnovers and dead screens drag a capable passer
report.take:
Shough is a second-year pocket passer for a 1-4 Saints team whose defense ranks 27th in EPA. He has thrown a lot, as the seventh-highest yardage total shows, but his efficiency sits in the bottom third. He is 32nd of 43 in yards per attempt and 28th in EPA per dropback. That looks like a quarterback who can't move the ball. The splits say something different. Every depth bucket that travels past the line of scrimmage is positive: +0.132 per play short, +0.437 intermediate, +0.195 deep. The negative total comes from what surrounds those throws.

Three things drain the value. The first is 30 throws behind the line at -0.408 EPA with a 23% success rate, and the targets on them show the cause. Alvin Kamara (-0.429 per target) and Bryce Lance (-0.953) have soaked up 33 targets that lose value almost every time. That is a play-design and personnel problem as much as a quarterback one. The second is ball security: 5 interceptions plus 3 lost fumbles, the latter ranking 40th of 43, including two lost against Las Vegas. The third is third down, at -0.222 EPA with an average of 8 yards to go. Five of his 13 sacks have come there, and a 39% conversion rate keeps cutting drives short.

The numbers also hide real progress. As a rookie he turned 41.9% of pressures into sacks, 48th of 62. This year it is 27.9%, and his bad-throw rate has dipped from 15.3% to 13.2%. He is more aggressive into tight windows (16.6% vs 12.8%) and still completing above expectation. In the red zone he has been excellent: 8 touchdowns, no interceptions, completions 11.4 points over expected. That will cool. But a quarterback who is efficient on throws past the line and good in the red zone is closer to average than his EPA rank suggests.

The week-to-week line is jagged. The Baltimore win (+10.9 EPA, 27 of 34) is what the ceiling looks like. The Week 5 dud (-11.9, 96 yards, two picks) came against the league's top-ranked defense and shouldn't be read as a collapse. With Jordyn Tyson out until November and Chris Olave carrying the passing game at +0.705 per target, the outlook depends on whether the offense stops spending plays on the flat and on Lance.

strengths.title: Efficient once the ball travels
strengths.body: Short, intermediate and deep throws all produce positive EPA. The intermediate range is the best at +0.437 per play, with 60% success. This is where his size and timing show, and it lines up with a CPOE above expectation for a second straight season. It is a repeatable skill rather than a hot streak.

strengths.title: Red-zone finishing
strengths.body: He has 8 red-zone touchdowns with no interceptions on 27 attempts, completing 11.4 points over expectation. That accounts for most of his 9 touchdowns and props up his fantasy line. The decision-making is real, but a perfect touchdown-to-interception ratio on 27 throws will regress.

strengths.title: Sacks under pressure way down
strengths.body: His pressure-to-sack rate fell from 41.9% as a rookie to 27.9%, moving him from near the bottom to the middle of the pack. His time to throw is steady at 2.75, so this looks like faster processing rather than simply holding the ball less. It is the clearest sign of second-year growth.

concerns.title: Turnovers, especially fumbles
concerns.body: He has 5 interceptions and 3 lost fumbles in five games, with 5 turnover-worthy fumbles charted. The interceptions come from every depth, not one bad habit. Fumble recoveries tend to even out, but the fumble count itself points to loose pocket handling, and that is a real flaw.

concerns.title: Behind-the-line throws are dead plays
concerns.body: His 30 attempts behind the line of scrimmage have averaged -0.408 EPA despite an 83% completion rate. The completions just don't gain yards. Much of this is the scheme and Kamara's -0.429 per target rather than Shough. Still, those 30 throws are about 15% of his attempts and drag his per-dropback numbers down.

concerns.title: Third-and-long stalls drives
concerns.body: On third down he is at -0.222 EPA with an 8-yard average to go and 5 sacks. A shaky early-down run game (offRushEpa 16th) puts him in long-yardage spots, so this is partly situational. Even so, a 39% conversion rate is why his yardage doesn't turn into points.

trend.note: His per-game passing EPA has swung from +10.9 at Baltimore to -11.9 against Minnesota, with three games between -3.6 and +0.7. The low point came against the league's top-ranked defense, so it doesn't mark a decline on its own.

nextGame.headline: Soft Giants pass rush meets a QB whose drives die on sacks
nextGame.body:
The Giants' defense ranks 22nd in EPA and 23rd against the pass. Their pass rush is among the weakest in the league: 28th in hit rate and 26th in sack rate. That attacks his biggest drain, the sacks and drive-killing third downs. The catch is deep coverage, where New York ranks 2nd in EPA allowed. Shough's best range is 10-19 yards, though, and the Giants are only middling on short throws (14th). They have also allowed 2.2 quarterback touchdowns a game, 26th, and their WR1 matchups have scored 5 PPR points over average, so Olave sets up well. Offenses run more than usual against them, but Saints game scripts have tilted toward passing because their own defense leaks.

Availability helps New Orleans. The Giants placed edge rusher Chauncey Golston (52% of snaps) on IR, thinning a rush that was already weak. Safety Jason Pinnock is out, and starting safety Tyler Nubin (83%) and corner Colton Hood are questionable. That could open seams against an otherwise stingy deep shell. On the Saints' side, Jordyn Tyson remains on IR, so targets stay concentrated on Olave, Vele and Juwan Johnson. Guard Jeremiah Wright's absence changes nothing, since he hasn't played a snap.

keyMatchups.title: Saints protection vs weak Giants rush
keyMatchups.body: Shough has taken 13 sacks and been hit or sacked on 16.5% of dropbacks. The Giants rank near the bottom in both hit and sack rate, and Golston's loss makes that worse. A cleaner pocket should lift his third-down results.

keyMatchups.title: Olave against the Giants' WR1 coverage
keyMatchups.body: Olave is his go-to target at +0.705 EPA on 54 targets. The Giants have let opposing WR1s exceed their averages by 5 PPR points, 28th in the league. Their WR1 EPA allowed is better (8th), so expect volume more than big plays.

keyMatchups.title: Intermediate game vs stingy deep shell
keyMatchups.body: New York has been the second-best defense against deep passes, so his 25 deep attempts at a 36% completion rate aren't the route to success here. The 10-19 window is, especially with both starting safeties banged up.

nextGame.watch: How the Saints convert on third down against a rush that rarely gets home. If his third-down sacks disappear, this is a 250-yard, multi-touchdown game. If they don't, the pass rush wasn't the problem.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume should hold. The Saints' defense ranks 27th in EPA and 28th against deep passes, so New Orleans will often be throwing to keep pace, and he has played every snap. The red-zone perfection and the pace of 3 lost fumbles in five games should both move toward the middle. Expect fewer touchdowns per red-zone trip, but also fewer giveaways from the fumble side. His yards per attempt should climb back toward his rookie 7.29 if the play-calling cuts the behind-the-line throws and Lance's targets. Tyson's expected November return is the clearest path to that.

The year-over-year improvement in avoiding sacks and in throw accuracy looks real. What separates a league-average season from another bottom-third one is interceptions: he has 5 in five games and 6 in ten last year. The bigger risk is that a losing record changes the picture. He isn't in any danger on the depth chart, but the losses will keep game scripts pass-heavy and sloppy.

bets.reason: The Giants rank 26th in sack rate and 28th in hit rate and just lost Golston to IR. Shough's pressure-to-sack rate has also improved sharply from his rookie year.
He averages 1.8 touchdowns a game behind 8 red-zone scores, and the Giants allow 2.2 quarterback touchdowns a game, 26th. A weak rush plus banged-up safeties should mean more sustained drives.
He has thrown picks in 3 of 5 games, from every depth, and ranks 31st in interception rate. The Giants' 23rd-ranked pass defense doesn't need to force turnovers for one to happen.

confidence.note: Five games, one prior season, and key splits on 25-40 plays
